title: Memorable job interviews
context: You will hear five short extracts in which people talk about a job interview they remember well.

unit.style: spontaneous and natural, as if talking to an interviewer, at a normal pace

turns.text: I'd applied for a job as a data analyst, and halfway through the interview they put a laptop in front of me and said, 'This spreadsheet is broken. You've got twenty minutes to fix it.' I'd never heard of that happening before. Then, about five minutes in, the laptop froze completely. My first instinct was to panic, but I took a breath, told them what I'd been trying to do and talked them through how I'd solve it on paper. They told me afterwards that it was my reaction that got me the job.

I walked into the room and nearly walked straight back out again, because the person interviewing me was a guy from my high school. Back then I'd written him off as the quiet, boring kid who never said anything, and I'm ashamed to say I wasn't always nice to him. Twelve years later, here he was, asking me the sharpest questions I've ever been asked. He was totally professional about it, and I did get the job. But it really made me think about how quickly I used to make up my mind about people.

Everything was going grand until the manager leaned back and asked me which kitchen appliance I'd be, and why. I genuinely thought she was joking. When I realised she wasn't, I said a toaster, because I'm reliable, I warm up quickly, and I occasionally set off the fire alarm. She laughed, and I relaxed. I found out later that the other candidates had far more experience than me. I think what made the difference was that I didn't apologise for who I was.

I'd expected to meet one person, so when I was shown into a room with six people sitting behind a long table, I was pretty thrown. They took turns firing questions at me, and I never knew who to look at. I didn't get the job, and I was gutted for about a week. But one of them rang me afterwards and gave me really detailed feedback, which was incredibly generous. I used every word of it in my next interview, and that time I was offered the position.

At the time I was applying for about ten jobs at once, and I'd got into the habit of using pretty much the same answers for all of them. Big mistake. Right at the start, I told the interviewer how much I admired the company, and then used the name of their main competitor. There was a terrible silence. I tried to laugh it off, but I knew it was over. These days I treat every application as if it's the only one, and I put in the hours before I walk through the door.

task1.prompt: TASK ONE · For questions 21–25, choose from the list (A–H) what happened at each speaker's interview.

options.B: They were asked an unusual question.
options.C: They met someone they already knew.
options.D: They had to do a practical task.
options.G: They were interviewed by a group.

task2.prompt: TASK TWO · For questions 26–30, choose from the list (A–H) what each speaker learnt from the experience.

options.B: to be honest about their weaknesses
options.C: not to judge people too quickly
options.D: to ask more questions of their own
options.E: that being yourself can matter more than experience
options.F: to stay calm when something goes wrong
options.G: that failure can lead to success
